blocks.content: Swapping is one of the oldest ideas in operating system memory management. Instead of moving small pieces of a process's memory in and out of RAM as needed, swapping moves a process's entire memory image out to disk all at once, and later moves that same entire image back in, all at once, before the process can run again.

This chapter sits inside the Memory Management module alongside Virtual Memory and Paging, and it exists specifically to draw a sharp line between swapping and demand paging, two mechanisms that sound similar but operate at genuinely different scales. By the end you should be able to state, precisely, exactly what makes swapping different from paging, why a system reaches for it, what it actually costs, and why it still matters even though demand paging handles most of the everyday work today.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408968776-564946678.png
1. What Swapping Actually Means

Demand paging, covered in the Virtual Memory and Paging chapters, moves memory in small fixed size pieces called pages, a few kilobytes at a time, fetching exactly the page a process touches and nothing more. Swapping works at a completely different scale. Rather than reasoning about individual pages, swapping picks an entire process and moves the whole thing, every page it owns, its complete memory image, out to disk in one single operation.

This whole process versus individual page distinction is the single most important thing to understand about swapping specifically. A page fault under demand paging touches one small piece of one process's memory. A swap out touches everything that process owns, all at once, leaving nothing of that process resident in RAM until it is swapped back in later, also all at once. Treating swapping and paging as the same mechanism under two different names is the most common mistake learners make with this topic.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Demand paging moves individual pages in and out of RAM as they are needed. Swapping moves an entire process's memory image out to disk at once, and later moves that same entire image back in at once, before the process can run again.

2. Why The OS Swaps An Entire Process Out
blocks.text: 2. Why The OS Swaps An Entire Process Out

blocks.content: A system swaps an entire process out typically because physical memory is under severe pressure. There are more ready processes wanting to run than can simultaneously fit inside the RAM actually installed on the machine, and simply evicting a handful of individual pages here and there is not enough to relieve that pressure.

When this happens, the operating system looks for a process that is currently idle or lower priority, one that is not actively needed right now, and swaps that entire process out. Because the whole process leaves RAM at once, this frees a large, useful chunk of memory in a single operation, room for one or more other ready processes to actually run, rather than freeing memory one small page at a time.

blocks.title: Who gets chosen
blocks.content: The OS favors an idle or lower priority process as the swap out candidate, since it is not needed immediately and swapping it out causes the least disruption to the processes that are actively doing useful work right now.
3. The Swap Space: A Dedicated Region of Disk
blocks.text: 3. The Swap Space: A Dedicated Region of Disk

blocks.content: Somewhere has to hold a process's entire memory image while it sits outside RAM, and that somewhere is the swap space, sometimes called the swap area. It is a dedicated, reserved region of disk, set aside specifically to hold swapped out process memory images, and it is kept separate from the regular file system that stores your files and folders.

A dedicated area is used rather than an arbitrary file for practical reasons. A reserved region gives the operating system a predictable location it can write to and read from without going through the full file system layer, and it can be organized ahead of time for the access pattern swapping actually needs, large sequential reads and writes, rather than the small scattered access pattern a general file system is tuned for.

blocks.content: 4. Worked Example: A Process Gets Swapped Out And Back In
blocks.text: 4. Worked Example: A Process Gets Swapped Out And Back In

blocks.content: Picture a system running several processes at once that suddenly hits real memory pressure, perhaps a new, memory hungry process just started and there simply is not enough free RAM to give it room. The operating system looks across the currently running processes and selects one that is lower priority and currently idle, not doing anything useful at this exact moment.

The OS writes that process's entire memory image, every page it owns, out to the swap area on disk in one operation, then marks all of that process's memory as free. That freed memory is now available for the new process, or for whichever processes actually need it right now. The swapped out process itself is completely paused, since it has no memory resident in RAM at all anymore.

Later, when the scheduler decides that swapped out process should run again, the operating system reads its entire memory image back from the swap area into RAM, all at once, before letting it resume. Only once that full image is back in place does the process continue executing, picking up exactly where it left off, unaware that any of this ever happened.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408968778-294754362.png
blocks.alt: Worked Example: A Process Gets Swapped Out And Back In

blocks.content: 5. The Real Cost Of Swapping

Moving an entire process's memory image is a large, slow disk operation. Its cost is directly proportional to the process's total memory footprint, so a process holding a few hundred megabytes takes far longer to swap out or swap in than a process holding only a few megabytes. Disk access is already orders of magnitude slower than a RAM access, and swapping asks for a huge amount of that slow disk access at once.

This is exactly why demand paging, moving only small individual pages as needed, largely replaced full process swapping as the everyday memory management mechanism in most modern general purpose systems. Demand paging only pays the disk access cost for the small handful of pages a process actually touches, instead of paying the full cost of that process's entire memory footprint every single time memory needs to be freed.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408968778-117623039.png

blocks.title: Cost, quantified honestly
blocks.content: A page fault under demand paging costs roughly the time to read one page from disk. A full process swap costs roughly the time to read or write that process's entire memory footprint, which can be hundreds or thousands of times larger.
6. Is Swapping Still Used Today

Full process swapping was the primary memory management mechanism on many early systems, back when physical memory sizes and workloads made it a reasonable everyday tool. Modern general purpose operating systems moved almost all of their everyday memory pressure handling to demand paging instead, precisely because of the cost difference described above.

That does not mean swapping disappeared entirely. Some systems still use swapping, or a page level variant that gets loosely called swapping even though it actually moves individual pages, as a last resort safety valve under extreme memory pressure, when demand paging alone cannot free memory fast enough. It remains conceptually important to understand even though it is far less central to everyday operation than it once was.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408968778-9962004.png
7. Relocation: Why A Swapped Process Must Be Able To Move
blocks.text: 7. Relocation: Why A Swapped Process Must Be Able To Move

blocks.content: Swapping a process out and later back in creates a requirement that is easy to overlook: the process must be relocatable, meaning it has to run correctly even if it comes back into a different physical location in RAM than the one it occupied before it was swapped out. There is no guarantee the exact same physical frames will be free again by the time that process is scheduled to return.

This connects directly back to address binding, covered in the Logical vs Physical Address chapter. Only run time address binding, where every memory access is translated live through the MMU using the process's current base register, safely supports a process being loaded back into a different physical location than where it was before being swapped out. Compile time or load time binding would fix the process to one physical location permanently, making it impossible to swap that process back in anywhere else.

blocks.content: 8. Common Mistakes And The Interview Angle
blocks.text: 8. Common Mistakes And The Interview Angle

blocks.content: A couple of misunderstandings come up often enough with this topic that they are worth naming directly before moving on.

["Using swapping and paging as if they were the same thing. They operate at genuinely different granularities, an entire process for swapping versus one individual page for paging, and the mechanisms, costs, and triggers that go with each are different too.","Assuming swapping is obsolete and never happens on modern systems. Demand paging handles the common case on most general purpose systems today, but swapping, or a page level variant loosely called by the same name, can still occur under real memory pressure as a last resort."]
items: Using swapping and paging as if they were the same thing. They operate at genuinely different granularities, an entire process for swapping versus one individual page for paging, and the mechanisms, costs, and triggers that go with each are different too.

Assuming swapping is obsolete and never happens on modern systems. Demand paging handles the common case on most general purpose systems today, but swapping, or a page level variant loosely called by the same name, can still occur under real memory pressure as a last resort.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to state the granularity difference between swapping and paging precisely: swapping moves an entire process's memory image at once, paging moves one individual page at a time. This exact distinction is a common point of confusion, and stating it cleanly and confidently is exactly what interviewers are listening for.

Swapping and demand paging both exist to solve the same underlying problem, more processes wanting memory than the machine physically has, but they solve it at very different scales. Keeping their granularity, cost, and triggers straight is what turns this topic from a vague memory into a precise, interview ready piece of operating systems knowledge.
